Measure of the three-dimensional space occupied by a region or enclosed by a surface. Volume is quantified with SI derived units such as the cubic metre and the [[Litre|litre]], or with imperial and U.S. customary units such as the [[Gallon|gallon]], quart and cubic inch. The volume of a container is generally understood as its capacity, the amount of gas or liquid it could hold, rather than the space the container itself displaces. Simple shapes have volumes given by arithmetic formulas; more complicated shapes can be handled with integral calculus if a formula exists for their boundary.

The earliest evidence of volume calculation comes from [[Ancient Egypt]] and [[Mesopotamia]], as problems approximating the volume of cuboids, cylinders, frustums and cones, preserved in the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (c. 1820 BC). The last three books of [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's *Elements*]] (c. 300 BC) gave exact formulas for parallelepipeds, cones, pyramids, cylinders and spheres. [[Archimedes]] devised approximate formulas for several shapes by the method of exhaustion.

The many volume units of the Middle Ages led [[Henry III of England]] to standardize them in the Assize of Bread and Ale (1258), which introduced the gallon and bushel. In the early 17th century Bonaventura Cavalieri applied the ideas of integral calculus to the volume of any object; Pierre de Fermat, [[Isaac Newton]], Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and others extended this in the 17th and 18th centuries into modern calculus.

On April 7, 1795, French law defined the metric system, including the litre (1 dm³) for liquids. In 1824 the imperial gallon was defined as the volume of ten pounds of water at 17 °C; the Weights and Measures Act 1985 fixed it at precisely 4.54609 litres.

American animator, film producer, voice actor and entrepreneur. Disney pioneered the American animation industry and introduced several developments in cartoon production. He holds the record for most [[Academy Awards]] won by (22) and nominated for (59) an individual.

Born in [[Chicago]] and raised largely in Missouri, he developed an early interest in drawing and moved to California in the early 1920s. With his brother Roy he founded the Disney Brothers Studio, now [[The Walt Disney Company|the Walt Disney Company]]. With Ub Iwerks he developed [[Mickey Mouse]] in 1928, his first major success; Disney voiced the character in the early years. The studio introduced synchronized sound, three-strip Technicolor and animated feature films, including [[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (film)|*Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs*]] (1937), [[Fantasia (1940 film)|*Fantasia*]] (1940) and [[Mary Poppins (film)|*Mary Poppins*]] (1964), which received five Academy Awards. His career also saw labor conflicts, including the 1941 animators' strike.

In July 1955 he opened [[Disneyland]] in Anaheim, California, funding it partly through television programs. In 1965 he began developing Disney World, centered on a planned city, the "Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow" (EPCOT). A heavy smoker, he died of lung cancer before either was completed.

He was shy in private, with a warm public persona and high standards. Accusations that he was racist or antisemitic have been contradicted by many who knew him. Historians have viewed him variously as a purveyor of homely patriotic values and as a representative of American cultural imperialism.

Armed conflict between the armed forces of states, or between governmental forces and armed groups organized under a command structure and able to sustain military operations, or between such organized groups. War is generally characterized by widespread violence, destruction and mortality, fought with regular or irregular forces, and its aims are typically political, economic or territorial. Warfare refers to the activities and characteristics of types of war, or of wars in general. Total war is warfare not restricted to legitimate military targets and can cause massive civilian suffering.

The English word derives from the 11th-century [[Old English]] *wyrre* and *werre*, from Old French *werre*, from Frankish *\*werra*, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *\*werzō* "mixture, confusion."

Anthropologists disagree about whether warfare was common throughout prehistory or arose later, after agriculture or organized states. It is hard to establish for the Paleolithic because few remains survive; evidence of violent conflict appears to increase in the Mesolithic, from about 10,000 years ago. In his 1996 book *War Before Civilization*, Lawrence H. Keeley estimates that approximately 90–95% of known societies engaged in at least occasional warfare. Since the rise of the state some 5,000 years ago, military activity has continued over much of the globe. The oldest known battlefield in Europe is thought to date to 1250 BC, and the [[Bronze Age]] has been described as a key period in the intensification of warfare. The use of [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] brought major changes to war itself. Charles Tilly argued that "war made the state, and the state made war."

Since 1945, great power wars, territorial conquests and war declarations have declined in frequency, wars have been increasingly regulated by international humanitarian law, and battle deaths have declined, partly owing to military medicine. Scholars debate whether war is in decline: Joshua Goldstein, John Mueller and Steven Pinker argue that it is, while Bear F. Braumoeller challenges the claim. [[Civil war|Civil wars]] have increased in absolute terms since 1945, and combat has largely been a matter of civil wars and insurgencies. The major interstate exceptions include the Korean War, the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971, the Iran–Iraq War, the Gulf War, the Eritrean–Ethiopian War and the Russo-Ukrainian War.

Types of warfare include asymmetric warfare, between belligerents of drastically different capability; [[Biological warfare]], using infectious agents or toxins; [[Chemical weapon|chemical warfare]], in which poison gas in World War I caused over a million estimated casualties, including more than 100,000 civilians; cold warfare, an intense rivalry without direct military conflict; conventional warfare; cyberwarfare; [[Insurgency|insurgency]], a rebellion by irregular forces against authority; information warfare; [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear warfare]]; radiological warfare; and total war. One estimate puts deaths from the 20th century's major conflicts at 100–231 million when direct violence, starvation, disease and related political decisions are combined.

Unwanted or unusable material, any substance discarded after primary use or regarded as worthless or defective. A by-product, by contrast, is a joint product of relatively minor economic value. A waste product may become a by-product, joint product or resource through an [[Invention|invention]] that raises its value above zero. Examples include municipal solid waste (household garbage), hazardous waste, wastewater, radioactive waste and others.

The Basel Convention (1989) defines wastes as substances or objects disposed of, intended to be disposed of, or required to be disposed of by national law. The [[European Union]]'s Waste Framework Directive (2008/98/EC) defines waste as "an object the holder discards, intends to discard or is required to discard."

The [[OECD]] defines municipal solid waste as "waste collected and treated by or for municipalities," typically household, commercial, and demolition or construction waste. In 2018 the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) concluded that 292.4 million short tons of municipal waste were generated, about 4.9 pounds per person per day; approximately 69 million tons were recycled and 25 million tons composted. Most collected household waste ends up in [[Landfill|landfills]]. The EPA estimated that the U.S. generated about 600 million tons of construction and demolition waste in 2018. U.S. hazardous waste, defined as waste capable of harming health or the environment, is regulated under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act.

Globally, municipal solid waste reached 2.24 billion tonnes in 2020, or 0.79 kg per person per day, and is projected to rise to 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. Only about 13.5% of waste is [[Recycling|recycled]] worldwide. Open dumping in developing areas contributes to methane emissions and [[Groundwater|groundwater]] contamination, and electronic waste exceeds 50 million tonnes yearly.

Inorganic compound with the chemical formula H₂O, a transparent, tasteless, odorless and nearly colorless liquid at room temperature. Water is the main constituent of Earth's streams, lakes and oceans and the fluid of all known living organisms, in which it acts as a solvent. It provides neither food energy nor organic micronutrients, yet it is vital to all known life. Because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid, it is often called the "universal solvent," though it dissolves nonpolar substances poorly. As found in nature it almost always contains dissolved substances, and special steps are needed to obtain chemically pure water.

The word comes from Old English *wæter*, from Proto-Germanic *\*watar*, from Proto-Indo-European *\*wod-or*.

Water is a polar molecule, and strong intermolecular [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen bonding]] largely determines its physical and chemical properties. Earth's surface temperature and pressure lie close to water's [[Triple point|triple point]], so water exists there as solid (ice), liquid and gas (water vapor or steam). Phase transitions are freezing, melting, vaporization, condensation, sublimation and deposition. At 1 atm, ice melts or water freezes at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C; the boiling point falls by 1 °C every 274 m of altitude. Temperatures exceed 205 °C in the geyser Old Faithful and can exceed 400 °C in [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]], where water stays liquid under pressure.

Water is unusual in expanding as it cools within certain temperature ranges. At 1 atm its maximum [[Density|density]], 999.972 kg/m³, occurs at 3.98 °C. On freezing it expands by about 9%, reaching 917 kg/m³, which can burst pipes and crack rocks. Because ice floats and insulates the water below, most aquatic organisms survive winter in lakes. This anomalous behavior is also part of the [[Thermohaline circulation|thermohaline circulation]] that distributes heat around the oceans. Water is diamagnetic.

Water covers about 71% of Earth's surface. Seas and [[Ocean|oceans]] hold about 96.5% of the volume, groundwater 1.7%, glaciers and ice caps of Antarctica and Greenland 1.7%, and the air (vapor, clouds and precipitation) 0.001%. It moves continuously through the [[Water cycle|water cycle]] of evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and runoff, usually reaching the sea.

Water is central to the world economy. Approximately 70% of the fresh water humans use goes to agriculture, and fishing provides 6.5% of global protein. Much long-distance trade moves by boat on seas, rivers, lakes and canals. Water, ice and snow are also used for cooling, heating, industry, cooking and washing, and in sports such as swimming, surfing, diving, ice skating and skiing.

Propagating dynamic disturbance, a change from equilibrium, of one or more quantities in a medium or field. Periodic waves oscillate repeatedly about an equilibrium value at some [[Frequency|frequency]]. Two identical periodic waves traveling in opposite directions superimpose to make a standing wave, which has nulls where the amplitude is small or zero. Viewed macroscopically, a wave is the dynamic response of a [[Field (physics)|field]] to effects that can only propagate at finite speed.

The two types most studied in classical physics are mechanical and electromagnetic waves. In a mechanical wave, stress and strain fields oscillate about a mechanical equilibrium, and the disturbance passes from particle to particle. Examples include [[Sound|sound]] waves, seismic waves generated by an [[Earthquake|earthquake]], surface waves and string vibrations. In an electromagnetic wave such as light, coupling between electric and magnetic fields sustains propagation according to [[Maxwell's equations]]. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum; by frequency they are called radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Other types include [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]], disturbances in spacetime, and plasma waves. Mechanical and electromagnetic waves transfer energy, momentum and information.

The simplest wave mathematically is a sinusoidal plane wave, in which the field undergoes [[Simple harmonic motion|simple harmonic motion]] at one frequency. A wave is transverse if the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and longitudinal if aligned with it. Electromagnetic plane waves are strictly transverse; sound waves in fluids are longitudinal. The orientation of the oscillation is the wave's [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]]. Wave speed relates to frequency and wavelength by v = fλ. In quantum mechanics, wave–particle duality means that entities such as electrons show both wave-like and particle-like behavior.

One of the four known fundamental interactions, acting between subatomic particles. The others are electromagnetism, the strong interaction and gravitation. The weak interaction, also called the weak force or weak nuclear force, is responsible for the radioactive [[Beta decay|beta decay]] of atoms and participates in nuclear fission and [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]]. First suggested in 1933, it reached its current form in the 1950s and 1960s, and Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam and Steven Weinberg shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for electroweak theory.

In the [[Standard Model]], the weak interaction has three carriers, the W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons ([[W and Z bosons]]), which were not discovered until 1983 at [[CERN]]. Their large mass, approximately 90 GeV/c², makes them short-lived and gives the force a very short effective range of around 10⁻¹⁷ to 10⁻¹⁶ m, less than the diameter of a proton. The force is termed weak because its field strength over a set distance is typically several orders of magnitude less than that of electromagnetism; its coupling constant lies between 10⁻⁷ and 10⁻⁶, against about 10⁻² for electromagnetism. The carriers' masses are explained in the Standard Model by the [[Higgs boson|Higgs mechanism]].

The weak interaction is unique in several respects. It is the only interaction that changes the flavour of [[Quark|quarks]] and leptons and the only one that violates parity symmetry. In beta-minus decay, a down quark in a neutron changes into an up quark, converting the neutron to a proton and emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. This conversion makes the weak interaction important in the fusion of hydrogen into helium in stars. Neutrinos interact only through gravity and the weak interaction.

Any implement or tool used to deter, threaten, inflict physical damage on, harm or kill. Weapons serve hunting, crime, law enforcement, self-defense and warfare. Ordinary objects such as rocks and bottles can serve as weapons, but many objects are designed for the purpose, from clubs and swords to firearms, tanks, artillery, missiles, chemical, biological and [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]]. In a broader sense a weapon may be anything used to gain a tactical, strategic, material or mental advantage over an adversary.

Weapons have driven cultural evolution, since users adapt to enemies' weapons in a continuing arms race. The earliest unambiguous weapons are the Schöningen spears, eight wooden throwing spears more than 300,000 years old.

Metal tools began with copper about 3,300 BC and were followed by the [[Bronze Age]] and its swords. The battering ram was in use by 2500 BC. Early iron swords were not superior to bronze ones; more important was the domestication of the horse and widespread use of spoked wheels by c. 2000 BC, which produced the light, horse-drawn [[Chariot|chariot]]. Chariots ceased to be militarily relevant by the 4th century BC. [[Cavalry]] developed once horses were bred to carry a human, and warships such as the trireme were in use by the 7th century BC.

Post-classical European warfare was dominated by [[Knight|knights]] supported by massed infantry, with infantry using spears, bows and later pikes. The introduction of [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] from Asia at the end of the period revolutionized warfare: musketeers protected by pikemen came to dominate open battles, and the cannon replaced the [[Trebuchet|trebuchet]] as the dominant siege weapon. Firearms differ from earlier weapons in releasing energy from combustible propellants rather than from a counterweight or spring.

State of the Earth's atmosphere at a specific place and time, described in terms of temperature, humidity, cloud cover and stability. On Earth most weather occurs in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere. Weather refers to day-to-day atmospheric conditions, whereas [[Climate|climate]] is their average over longer periods.

Weather is driven by differences in air pressure, temperature and moisture from place to place. These differences arise partly from the Sun's angle, which varies with latitude. The strong temperature contrast between polar and tropical air gives rise to the largest atmospheric circulations: the [[Hadley cell]], the Ferrel cell, the polar cell and the [[Jet stream|jet stream]]. Mid-latitude systems such as [[Extratropical cyclone|extratropical cyclones]] are caused by instabilities of the jet stream flow. Because Earth's axis is tilted relative to the ecliptic, sunlight arrives at different angles through the year, producing seasons, and annual surface temperatures usually range ±40 °C. Over thousands of years, changes in Earth's orbit affect the solar energy received and influence long-term climate ([[Milankovitch cycles]]). Surface temperature differences create pressure differences, and air moving from higher to lower pressure forms wind.

Weather forecasting applies science and technology to predict the state of the atmosphere at a future time and place. Numerical weather prediction, which began in the mid-20th century, has raised short-term reliability to approximately 90% accuracy for five-day outlooks, but the weather system is chaotic: small changes can grow into large effects, which limits predictability beyond about two weeks.

Jupiter's [[Great Red Spot]] is an anticyclonic storm known to have existed for at least 300 years.

Government support intended to ensure that members of a society can meet basic human needs such as food and shelter. Social security may be synonymous with welfare, or refer specifically to social insurance programs, which support only prior contributors (for example pensions), as opposed to social assistance, given on the basis of need alone. More broadly, welfare can include subsidized healthcare, education, vocational training and public housing. In a [[Welfare state|welfare state]], the state assumes responsibility for such services. Articles 22 and 25 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] assert a right to social security and an adequate standard of living.

Some historians view codified almsgiving, such as the zakat policy of the Rashidun caliph [[Umar]] (634), as an early example of universal government welfare. Welfare existed under Urukagina of [[Mesopotamia]]. In the Roman Empire, [[Augustus]] provided a monthly grain dole, the *Cura Annonae*, for citizens unable to afford food. The [[Song dynasty]] government supported state hospitals, orphanages and free pharmacies. One study called the 18th-century Qing relief system, based on granaries used to stabilize food prices, "the most elaborate relief system in world history."

From the 14th century Italian city governments partnered with the church to provide welfare and education. In 1523 Martin Luther devised a "Common Chest" plan for Leisnig, Saxony, and free imperial cities of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] managed welfare through city governments.

The first welfare state was Imperial Germany (1871–1918), where the Bismarck government introduced social security in 1889. The United Kingdom introduced it around 1913 and adopted the welfare state with the National Insurance Act 1946, under the Attlee government (1944–1951).
